content_layers.observation_text: Objects may return in a bag, stay on the body, be removed before cremation, become evidence, get inventoried, or become contested; the object path often carries grief.
content_layers.source_synthesis: Public sources support this as body-after-death / disposition-chain vocabulary: authority, paperwork, custody, cost, provider, autopsy, donation, and disposition words appear in family rooms after death, but they do not authorize a public instruction page.
content_layers.witness_language: Families may hear ordinary words such as release, funeral home, viewing, cremation, ashes, autopsy, certificate, permit, donation, urn, interment, or disposition before they understand who has authority or what those words require.
content_layers.reader_boundary: This route can orient a reader to language and limits; it cannot tell them what to choose, what is legal where they live, what a provider will do, what a body will look like, or whether a donation/autopsy/disposition is available.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: Future public rendering requires funeral/regulatory, legal/jurisdictional, ethics, privacy, cultural/tradition, clinical if applicable, official-trace if applicable, and publication-language review.
language_notes: Keep body, person, decedent, remains, and loved-one language context-sensitive rather than flattening all terms into one style rule.
Separate family grief language from provider paperwork language and official trace language.
Avoid procedure steps, price promises, legal rights advice, and provider recommendations.
content_layers.what_this_is_not: Not funeral advice, not legal advice, not medical advice, not autopsy advice, not body-donation advice, not organ/tissue donation advice, not consumer shopping advice, not a recommendation about burial, cremation, green burial, alkaline hydrolysis, natural organic reduction, embalming, viewing, or transport.
